vignette:
He is 69 now, a plumber who still wakes before dawn out of habit, moving quietly through the kitchen so he does not disturb his wife. He measures the morning by sounds—the kettle beginning to hum, the pipes ticking in the walls, a motorbike passing outside—and he notices before his feet touch the floor whether his body has slept or only gone still for a few hours. Most nights he says he does not really rest. He drops into sleep and then rises out of it suddenly, heart pounding, already alert, as if someone has called his name in the dark.

When he was a young man in Southeast Asia, long before he came to the United States, he was taken and held for months during a period of political violence in his home region. He does not begin there when he first talks. At first he speaks around it, saying only that there was “a camp,” that men disappeared, that hunger became ordinary. Over several meetings he describes a bamboo room with no clock and almost no light, the smell of wet earth, sweat, and rusted metal. He remembers being watched while eating, being ordered to sit still for hours, being struck unpredictably. What stays with him most is not a single beating but the helplessness of waiting—never knowing when the door would open, never knowing what would happen next. He learned to listen for footsteps and changes in breathing. He learned that hope had to be kept very small.

After his release, he returned to what remained of ordinary life, but ordinary life no longer felt trustworthy. He married, worked, emigrated, and built a reputation as a dependable plumber, the kind of man who shows up on time and solves problems other people do not want to touch. He likes the logic of pipes: pressure builds, a joint fails, a blockage backs everything up, and if you know where to look, you can fix it. He says water tells the truth. People do not always.

For years he kept himself busy enough not to think. He took emergency calls, crawled under houses, replaced hot water heaters, worked through weekends. His wife came to understand that idleness made him uneasy. If he sat too long, he became distant or irritable. If she asked what was wrong, he would say “nothing” too quickly. He tells himself he survived by not dwelling on the past, but the past enters anyway. The metallic clang of a dropped tool can send a jolt through him before he knows why. Being in a cramped crawl space with poor air and one narrow exit can make his chest tighten. He keeps a flashlight in his hand even when there is enough light, and he positions his body so he can see the opening. On one job, a homeowner casually shut the basement door above him to keep out the cold. He was suddenly not in a basement anymore. He was back in confinement, breath shallow, hands slick, scrambling up the ladder so fast he banged his shoulder on a pipe. He laughed it off afterward and said he was feeling overheated, but he went home early and sat in his truck for nearly an hour before starting the engine.

At night the memories return less as a coherent story than as fragments. A door opening. Mud under bare feet. The sensation of being unable to stretch his legs. He sometimes shouts in his sleep in a language his grown children do not understand. His wife says he swings his arm as if pushing someone away. On those nights he wakes ashamed and goes to check the locks, then the windows, then the back door again. He knows his house is safe. Knowing does not settle his body.

He avoids documentaries about war and will leave the room if the news shows prisoners, blindfolds, or men with guns. He dislikes crowded waiting rooms and restaurants where someone can stand behind him. Family members describe him as hardworking and generous, but also strict, easily startled, and hard to get close to. His grandchildren climb onto his lap without hesitation, and he softens with them, yet even then he scans the room when voices get too loud. He does not like his wife to see him cry, but lately he has found himself doing so unexpectedly—while repairing an old valve, while smelling mildew in a flooded basement, while watching his grandson complain about being bored and feeling, all at once, anger and grief for the young man he used to be.

He says captivity taught him never to depend on anyone, yet age is confronting him with limits he cannot outwork. His knees ache on the job. He forgets small things and then worries he is losing control. With more time at home, there is less distance from memory. He speaks of guilt too: for surviving when others did not, for leaving his country, for how often fear made him hard with his children. Even now, sitting in a quiet office, he chooses the chair nearest the door. He notices every sound in the hallway. He tells the story carefully, in pieces, pausing often, as though opening one sealed room at a time.
